technique_notes.heading: Capo 2 — Shapes vs. Sounds
technique_notes.body: Clip your capo at the 2nd fret. Every fret number in this tab is relative to the capo — so 'fret 0' means the capoed string, and your open G shape here sounds as an A major to anyone with a tuner out. Play what your fingers see, not what the tuner reads.

technique_notes.heading: The Frozen Top Two Strings
technique_notes.body: Notice that strings 1 and 2 (high e and B) stay at frets 3 and 3 across ALL four chords — G, Em7, Dsus4, and A7sus4. This is Noel Gallagher's signature trick: anchor fingers 3 and 4 on those two strings and never lift them. If you're scrambling between chords, you're doing too much work — your anchor fingers shouldn't move at all.

technique_notes.heading: Downstroke-Rest Pattern
technique_notes.body: Each beat in this tab is a downstroke followed by an eighth-note rest — that rest is NOT silence you ignore, it's the groove. Let the strum ring for the first eighth, then damp or just stop the strum naturally before the next beat. The pattern is: DOWN-pause, DOWN-pause, DOWN-pause, DOWN-pause — four times per bar. Don't rush into the next hit; the space is what gives it the Oasis lurch.

technique_notes.heading: G → Em7 Change: Only Two Fingers Move
technique_notes.body: Going from G to Em7, your anchor fingers (3 and 4) stay frozen on strings 1-2. Release string 6 entirely (mute it), then slide finger 1 from string 5 fret 2 to hold strings 5 and 4 at fret 2. That's it — two fingers adjust, two fingers don't move. If the change feels slow, you're probably lifting your anchor unnecessarily.

technique_notes.heading: Dsus4 → A7sus4: One-Finger Swap
technique_notes.body: Dsus4 and A7sus4 are almost identical shapes: the only difference is that A7sus4 opens string 1 (lift finger 4 off the high e). Your anchor on string 2 (finger 3) stays put, and string 3 stays at fret 2 (finger 1). Practice just that lift in isolation — place the Dsus4 shape, lift finger 4, replace it. That micro-move is what distinguishes the two chords.

drills.name: Anchor and Lock the Top Two Strings
drills.what: Plant fingers 3 and 4 on strings 1-2 at fret 3 (the anchor that never moves in the intro) and strike the full G shape. The goal is to feel that anchor lock in before you ever attempt a chord change.
drills.success_criterion: Every string rings clean on each strike with zero buzzing, and your anchor fingers never visibly lift between repetitions.
drills.common_trap: Players tense up the whole hand trying to hold the anchor — the anchor fingers should be firm, the rest of the hand stays relaxed.

drills.name: G → Em7 Change with Frozen Anchor
drills.what: Move between G and Em7 as heard in the intro's first two bars, keeping fingers 3 and 4 welded to strings 1-2. Only the bass-side fingers adjust — feel the anchor hold the whole transition together.
drills.success_criterion: The chord change lands clean on beat 3 with no gap in sound and no buzzing — strings 1 and 2 ring identically through both chords.
drills.common_trap: Lifting the anchor fingers to 'reset' — keep them down the entire measure, even during the change.

drills.name: Dsus4 → A7sus4 One-Finger Lift
drills.what: Drill the Dsus4-to-A7sus4 swap heard in bars 3-4 of the intro. The only move is lifting finger 4 off string 1 to open it — everything else stays frozen. This isolates the smallest change in the whole progression.
drills.success_criterion: The open high e on A7sus4 rings with the same volume as the fretted notes — no muting, no hesitation between shapes.
drills.common_trap: Accidentally muting string 1 on Dsus4 by letting finger 4 sit flat instead of arched — arch all fingertips.

drills.name: Four-Bar Downstroke Groove
drills.what: Lock in the DOWN-rest strumming pulse used throughout the verse. Each beat is a crisp downstroke on the G shape followed by a deliberate eighth rest — the pause is the groove, not dead time. This prepares the verse's rhythmic feel before you add chord changes.
drills.success_criterion: Four downstrokes per bar lock perfectly with the click, and the gaps between strokes are even — it feels like a pulse, not a stumble.
drills.common_trap: Trying to fill the rest with an upstroke — resist it. Oasis's power comes from the downstroke-only commitment.
